questions.q: Why does a GPU instance carry a much higher on-demand hourly rate than a comparable general-purpose CPU VM?
options: Cloud providers apply an arbitrary surcharge to any instance with 'GPU' in its name, with no underlying cost driver
GPU instances always include more RAM than CPU VMs, and RAM is the only real cost driver
Specialized silicon, expensive high-bandwidth memory, high-speed interconnects, and constrained supply relative to CPU hardware drive the premium
GPU instances are billed in a different currency structure that inflates the displayed rate
questions.explain: The GPU premium comes from real cost drivers: specialized, low-volume silicon, HBM, interconnects like NVLink, and supply that has lagged demand — not an arbitrary label-based surcharge.

questions.q: Why is an idle GPU instance a categorically bigger budget problem than an idle standard CPU VM?
options: Idle GPU instances automatically scale themselves up, which idle CPU VMs cannot do
GPU instances cannot be stopped once started, so idling is unavoidable
Idle CPU VMs are billed at zero cost while idle GPU instances are not
The same hours of waste happen at a per-hour rate that is an order of magnitude or more above a CPU VM's rate, so the same mistake costs far more
questions.explain: Both an idle GPU and an idle CPU VM waste the same wall-clock time, but the GPU's much higher hourly rate turns that waste into a far larger dollar amount for the same duration.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why does a stuck or duplicated job on a multi-GPU training cluster create a much larger cost incident than the same mistake on a single CPU VM?
options: Multi-GPU clusters bill a flat fee regardless of how many GPUs are actually running
The mistake multiplies against however many GPUs the job spans, and each GPU already carries the high per-unit premium
Multi-GPU clusters are immune to stuck jobs because of built-in hardware safeguards
AWS and Azure refund any spend caused by a stuck multi-GPU job automatically
questions.explain: A mistake on a job spanning eight GPUs burns eight GPUs' worth of the already-high per-unit rate for every hour it runs unnoticed — the blast radius scales with the GPU count.

questions.q: What does 'cost velocity' refer to in the context of GPU spend?
options: How fast spend can accumulate per unit of time, which is much higher for GPU workloads than for standard compute
How quickly a cloud provider processes a refund request
The network throughput, in gigabits per second, between GPUs in a cluster
The rate at which GPU hardware depreciates on the provider's balance sheet
questions.explain: Cost velocity describes how quickly dollars accumulate per hour of inattention. Because GPU rates are so much higher per unit, the same delay in catching a problem costs far more on GPU infrastructure.

questions.q: Why does the lesson avoid stating exact current GPU instance prices when illustrating the cost gap versus CPU VMs?
options: Because GPU pricing is a trade secret that cannot legally be discussed

Because exact prices vary by region, generation, and cloud, and change often enough that a memorized figure would quickly become inaccurate — illustrative ratios build the right intuition without a false sense of precision
Because GPU instances are never billed per hour, only per month
Because no cloud provider publishes GPU pricing publicly
questions.explain: The lesson deliberately uses rough, clearly-labeled illustrative ratios rather than presenting specific dollar figures as if they were stable facts, since real pricing shifts by region, generation, and over time.
